description: The four lines a result is built from. A crawler that reaches the page reads these before it reads anything else, and a person in a results list reads nothing but these.

gates.title: Every Route Sets A Title
gates.rule: Each route sets its own title, whether by a title tag or the framework's metadata. A route with no title of its own inherits the layout's, and a whole site ranks under one name.
gates.fix: Set a title per route - a title tag, a metadata export, or whatever this stack uses.

gates.title: Titles Fit The Result
gates.rule: A title runs 30 to 60 characters. Under 30 it wastes the most valuable line on the page; over 60 Google truncates it mid-phrase and the reader never sees the end.
gates.fix: Rewrite the long ones to lead with the subject and put the brand last.

gates.title: No Two Routes Share A Title
gates.rule: Every title is distinct. Two routes with one title are two results a person cannot tell apart, and two pages the crawler treats as candidates for the same query.
gates.fix: Give each route a title naming what that route is, not what the site is.

gates.title: Every Route Sets A Description
gates.rule: Each route sets a meta description. Without one the result shows whatever fragment of body copy happens to match the query, which is rarely the sentence worth showing.
gates.fix: Write a description per route saying what the page does and why to open it.

gates.title: Descriptions Fit The Result
gates.rule: A description runs 120 to 160 characters. Shorter leaves the snippet half empty; longer is cut at the truncation point, which is usually mid-sentence.
gates.fix: Trim or extend each one so the whole sentence survives the cut.

gates.title: No Two Routes Share A Description
gates.rule: Every description is distinct. A description repeated across a site describes the site, which is not what a person scanning results is deciding between.
gates.fix: Rewrite the duplicates around what each route specifically offers.

gates.title: The Document Declares Its Language
gates.rule: The root element carries a lang attribute. Screen readers pick a voice from it, hreflang is meaningless without it, and a mismatched language is a reason to be shown to the wrong audience.
gates.fix: Set lang on the html element in the document shell.

gates.title: The Document Declares Its Charset
gates.rule: A charset declaration sits in the head. Without it the browser guesses, and a guess that lands wrong turns every non-ASCII character in a title into noise.
gates.fix: Add `<meta charset="utf-8">` as the first element in the head.

gates.title: The Document Declares Its Viewport
gates.rule: The shell sets a viewport. Mobile is the primary crawler, and a page without one renders at desktop width on a phone and is judged on that.
gates.fix: Add `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` to the shell.
